zh.question: 沿同一条路线经过黑洞，平均密度不同的类地球与类木星行星会怎样？
zh.observe: 固定路线，切换两种行星比较潮汐尺度和形变；再从上方跟踪长尾与回返路径，切近景观察橙色亮处怎样变化。

academic.title: 平均密度决定抗潮汐的尺度
academic.body: 在牛顿近似中，自引力维持的天体抵抗潮汐的能力与平均密度相关。粗略潮汐半径可写作rₜ≈R(M/m)^(1/3)；用m≈4πρR³/3替换后，同一黑洞下rₜ随ρ^(−1/3)变化。因此密度较低的天体往往在更远处受强烈影响。该关系省略与内部结构相关的系数，不能直接判定所有材料的破碎阈值。

academic.title: 轨道和结构必须一起比较
academic.body: 穿透因子β=rₜ/rₚ把潮汐半径与最近距离联系起来，β较大意味着经过得相对更深。为了比较密度，应先保持路线不变；为了比较轨道，再固定行星种类。真实结果还受内部层结、自转、强度和遭遇速度影响。可见的形变不等于完全破坏，脱离物质、剩余核心和逃逸部分应分别观察。

academic.title: 回返不等于成盘，变暗不等于吞入
academic.body: 碎屑可具有不同的轨道能量和角动量，一部分逃逸，一部分沿偏心轨道回返。真实相遇和激波可能使物质受热，但不保证立即形成完整圆盘。本例检测束缚碎屑外行后转向内行，再用温和耗散近似轨道变化；局部橙色亮度随近似能量损失增加，也会衰减。淡线仅记录少量物质点的最近路径。亮度不是温度、质量吞入率或真实光谱，也没有计算岩石断裂、气压和汽化。

zh.misconception: 低密度不等于“更轻就必然掉进去”；回返也不等于立刻形成圆盘。淡线是最近走过的路径，橙色亮处不是温度计。
zh.boundary: 同一批物质点用渐弱支撑和中心引力展示形变与释放，在束缚碎屑回返后启用简化耗散，保留偏心绕行。没有求解岩石断裂、气压、汽化、真实碰撞或相对论流体，也不预测某颗已知行星的瓦解、成盘或吞入比例。

narration.label: 挑一个旅行伙伴
narration.text: 今天换行星来做旅行伙伴。一个是类地球的岩石世界，另一个是类木星的气态世界。在这个比较里，它们的平均密度不同。先看看比较远的路线：经过得远还是近，会影响拉扯的强弱。行星自己的结构也很重要，但这个小模型还不能把岩石怎样裂开、气体怎样流动都算出来。
narration.cue: 从岩石行星、较远路线开始。

narration.label: 只换一个条件
narration.text: 我们做个小比较：让路线保持一样，只换行星的种类。请先暂停，猜一猜，哪一个更容易被拉开？过一会儿再播放到最靠近黑洞的地方。看看外层有没有离开，里面是不是还留着一团。这样比较，比一下把所有按钮都换掉更容易找到原因。
narration.cue: 同一路线切两种行星；停顿约四秒后看最近处。

narration.label: 跟着物质绕回来
narration.text: 继续跟着原来的物质。有些拉成长长的尾巴，有些走过一段弯路，又绕回来。回来不等于马上掉进去，也不等于已经排成圆盘。从上方看一看，哪些弯路拉得比较长？淡淡的线记下少量物质刚走过的路，不是又出现了一圈实体环。
narration.cue: 切俯视，慢慢跟踪长尾、偏心回返与最近路径。

narration.label: 看亮处，再作比较
narration.text: 切到近景，找一找橙色亮处。真实的物质相遇时可能碰撞、变热；这里用亮度变化帮助我们想象，但没有量出温度。变暗时，物质也可能还在继续绕行。现在再用同一种行星试试更远的路线：它是不是保留了更多原来的样子？这个比较帮助我们理解潮汐，不是在预报地球的未来。
narration.cue: 观察橙色亮处与衰减，再固定行星种类对照远近路线。

en.question: How would Earth-like and Jupiter-like planets with different mean densities respond along the same black-hole encounter?
en.observe: Keep the route fixed and compare tidal scale and deformation for both planets. Then track the tail and returning paths from above, and inspect changing orange patches in the close-up.

academic.title: Density sets a tidal scale
academic.body: In a Newtonian approximation, resistance of a self-gravitating body to tides depends on mean density. An order-of-magnitude radius is rₜ≈R(M/m)^(1/3). Substituting m≈4πρR³/3 gives rₜ proportional to ρ^(−1/3) for the same black hole. Lower-density bodies may be affected farther out. Structure-dependent coefficients are omitted, so this is not a universal material failure threshold.

academic.title: Compare orbit and structure separately
academic.body: The penetration factor β=rₜ/rₚ compares tidal radius with closest approach. Larger β means a relatively deeper encounter. Hold the route fixed when comparing density, then hold planet type fixed when comparing routes. Internal layers, spin, strength, and encounter speed also matter. Deformation is not identical to total destruction; inspect released material, the remaining core, and escaping fragments separately.

academic.title: Returning is not disk formation; fading is not capture
academic.body: Debris has different orbital energies and angular momenta. Some escapes, while some returns on eccentric orbits. Physical interactions and shocks may heat the material, without immediately creating a complete disk. Here, gentle dissipation starts after bound debris turns inward following outward motion. Local orange brightness responds to the approximate energy loss and also decays. Faint lines mark a few samples’ recent paths. Brightness is not a temperature, accretion rate or physical spectrum; rock fracture, gas pressure and vaporization are not calculated.

en.misconception: Low density does not mean that being lighter makes a body inevitably fall in. Returning does not instantly make a disk. Faint lines show recent paths, and orange patches are not thermometers.
en.boundary: One material population uses weakening support and central gravity to illustrate deformation and release, with simplified dissipation after bound debris returns and eccentric motion retained. The model does not solve rock fracture, gas pressure, vaporization, physical collisions or relativistic fluid dynamics, or predict a known planet’s disruption, disk formation or captured fraction.

narration.label: Choose a traveler
narration.text: Today a planet is our traveler: an Earth-like rocky world or a Jupiter-like gas world. In this comparison, they have different mean densities. Start with the more distant route: the distance of the pass changes the strength of the tides. A planet’s own structure matters too, but this small model cannot calculate all the ways rock breaks or gas flows.
narration.cue: Begin with the rocky planet on a distant route.

narration.label: Change one thing
narration.text: Let’s keep the route the same and change only the kind of planet. Pause and predict which might be pulled apart more easily. Then play to the closest point. Have outer layers left? Is a central clump still together? Changing one thing at a time makes the comparison easier to understand.
narration.cue: Compare both planets on one route; pause four seconds before closest approach.

narration.label: Follow the returning material
narration.text: Keep following the original material. Some stretches into a long tail. Some follows a curved path and returns. Coming back does not mean falling straight in or already forming a disk. Look from above: which paths are more stretched out? Faint lines record the recent paths of a few pieces of material. They are not new solid rings.
narration.cue: Use the top view to follow the tail, eccentric returns and recent paths slowly.

narration.label: Inspect the glow, then compare
narration.text: Use the close-up to find orange patches. Real material may collide and heat up when it meets other material. The changing brightness helps us imagine this, but it is not a temperature measurement. Material can keep orbiting even as its glow fades. Now try the farther route with the same planet. Does it keep more of its original shape? This comparison helps us understand tides; it is not a forecast of Earth’s future.
narration.cue: Observe orange patches and fading, then hold planet type fixed while comparing near and far routes.
